title: How an Atlanta Suburb Ended Up Sharing Flock Data With More Than 2,000 Organizations
gist: License-plate surveillance vendor Flock Safety's interconnected data-sharing network has grown so large that a single 67,000-person Atlanta suburb's camera data is accessible to over 2,000 outside organizations, with default settings, an opaque 'Nationwide lookup' tool, and a state-by-state regulatory patchwork repeatedly causing agencies to unknowingly share data beyond their intended scope -- prompting Flock to announce reactive governance changes amid a wave of officer-misuse scandals.

insights.claim: Alpharetta, Georgia -- a suburb of about 67,000 people served by roughly 120 police officers, with several dozen Flock Safety license-plate cameras -- has its camera data accessible to more than 2,000 police departments, colleges, airports, and government agencies nationwide, and separately receives data from more than 1,300 outside entities.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: Demonstrates how Flock's core product -- a network-effect data-sharing platform -- causes even a small local deployment to become a node in a nationwide surveillance web, which is central to evaluating both Flock's growth model and its regulatory/reputational risk exposure.
insights.locator: Data captured by those Flock cameras

insights.claim: Alpharetta's Flock data-sharing network has expanded rapidly in the past year: the number of entities receiving its data grew about 42% and the number of entities sending it data grew about 125% since June 2025.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: A concrete year-over-year growth rate for network connections is a proxy metric for the expansion of Flock's core interconnection product, relevant to assessing the company's growth trajectory and the pace at which surveillance scope is expanding largely without proportional oversight.
insights.locator: Alpharetta's data-sharing network has expanded tremendously

insights.claim: A Kentucky airport authority, the Louisville Regional Airport Authority, operates just 13 Flock cameras but shares data with 2,240 agencies nationwide and receives data from 1,124, showing Flock's customer base extends well beyond local policing into transportation and critical infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: Illustrates that Flock's addressable market and surveillance footprint extend into non-law-enforcement critical infrastructure operators, broadening both its commercial opportunity and its data-governance risk surface.

insights.claim: Flock's 'Nationwide lookup' tool, introduced in 2021, lets any opted-in customer query any other Flock customer nationwide by license plate; multiple agencies, including Reynoldsburg, Ohio and Palo Alto, California, discovered years after the fact that the tool had been silently enabled for them without their knowledge, in some cases as early as 2023.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: A default-on configuration for a national data-sharing tool that customers didn't realize was active is a specific product-design and consent failure that has directly caused compliance incidents and public controversy for Flock.
insights.locator: Often, the confusion has been tied to Flock's Nationwide lookup tool

insights.claim: California state law forbids sharing automatic license plate reader (ALPR) data with federal or out-of-state law enforcement, yet Palo Alto police officials say they only learned in December 2025 that Flock's Nationwide lookup tool had been active for their department since mid-2023, despite this being illegal under state law; Flock disputes the timeline and says it disabled the tool for California agencies by March 2025.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: A concrete instance of a Flock customer potentially violating state law due to vendor-side default settings represents direct legal exposure both for the customer agency and reputationally for Flock, and highlights the gap between contractual compliance claims and actual product configuration.
insights.locator: Notably, California law forbids sharing ALPR data

insights.claim: Flock disabled the Nationwide lookup tool for federal agencies following public backlash over the company's pilot program with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: Direct evidence that past political and reputational backlash materially altered Flock's product access controls shows the company is responsive to public pressure, a pattern relevant to anticipating how future controversies could similarly force product changes.
insights.locator: It allows any Flock customer to query

insights.claim: Query scope is left largely to individual officer discretion and varies wildly: a Reynoldsburg, Ohio officer queried 53 Flock networks for one search, then queried 5,392 networks 40 minutes later under the identical case code, with no explanation recorded in the log; the city attorney says officers 'typically... search every network they have access to' rather than narrowing scope.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: Shows weak internal controls over query scope at the individual-officer level, meaning stated agency-level data-sharing limits may not translate into disciplined actual usage, a governance risk relevant to civil-liberties and legal-liability assessments of Flock deployments.

insights.claim: In California, where ALPR sharing law is comparatively strict, the Northern California Regional Intelligence Center (NCRIC) fusion center's Flock network is limited to fewer than 400 in-state agencies, versus Alpharetta's 2,300+ node network in Georgia; yet NCRIC member agencies still ran more than 57,000 Flock queries in a single month (Nov 26-Dec 26, 2025), with over 96% of queries probing at least 100 networks.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: Shows state regulation effectively caps the breadth of Flock's network (fewer connected agencies) but does not meaningfully constrain query volume or intensity, an important nuance for evaluating how much state ALPR laws actually limit surveillance activity versus just network topology.
insights.locator: The effects of California's restrictions are visible

insights.claim: Twenty-four US states plus Washington, DC have statutes covering ALPR use, with wide variation in strictness -- for example, Illinois has barred law enforcement from using ALPR data in immigration or abortion-related criminal cases since 2023 -- creating a fragmented regulatory environment that directly shapes how large individual agencies' Flock data-sharing networks can become.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: A fragmented, state-by-state regulatory patchwork is a material and ongoing risk factor for Flock's network-effect business model, since new or tightened state ALPR laws could constrain data-sharing scope and reduce the value proposition state-by-state.

insights.claim: Following a surge of news coverage about officers misusing its technology, Flock announced changes on August 13, including recommending a reduced default ALPR data retention period of 7 days (down from 30), though customers can still pay for extended retention; requiring a criminal case code for every search; and mandating that by year-end all customers activate an 'Audit Assistance' tool that automatically suspends access when it detects abnormal search behavior.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: A reactive product-governance overhaul under public pressure is a pattern typical of controversial surveillance vendors self-regulating only after scandal, and represents a concrete, testable commitment (mandatory audit tooling by year-end) to track for actual implementation.
insights.locator: On August 13, Flock announced a set of changes

insights.claim: Multiple police departments across the country -- including Alpharetta, Reynoldsburg, Bibb County, Savannah, and Dallas -- have had officers resign or face investigation this year over alleged Flock misuse; Alpharetta's own newly activated Audit Assistance tool triggered an investigation on July 20 that led to an officer's resignation on August 5.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: A cluster of contemporaneous misuse scandals across multiple, geographically distinct Flock customer agencies within the same year signals a broadening, systemic reputational and regulatory risk for the company rather than an isolated incident, relevant to assessing customer-retention and legislative risk.

insights.claim: When agencies asked Flock why Nationwide lookup had been enabled without their knowledge, Flock's explanations were inconsistent and vague -- citing an 'event-log limitation' preventing it from confirming exactly when a feature was activated prior to February 2025, and describing nationwide sharing as 'a common default configuration for agencies' before the company added 'stronger in-product disclosures and tighter controls.'
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: Weak internal audit-logging capability and admitted use of unclear default configurations undercut Flock's ability to give customers -- and by extension the public -- a reliable account of how their data has been shared, a governance-maturity risk factor for a vendor selling into a trust-dependent, highly regulated government market.
